title_en: Laila Khawaja on how the Jensen Huang saga resets the US-China tech rivalry
content_en:
The Gavekal Technologies research director says the chip CEO’s removal and reinstatement has boosted China’s case for technological self-reliance.
Illustration: Lau Ka-kuen
Laila Khawaja is research director at Gavekal Technologies, the financial services and analytics firm’s tech wing. Before her current role, she worked at Gavekal Fathom China from its founding in 2009, developing broad expertise in China’s corporate landscape. A graduate of Beijing Foreign Studies University and Harvard University, she is currently based in Miami.
In this interview, Khawaja discusses the whirlwind dismissal and restoration of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, how that saga and other recent events have reframed the US-China tech rivalry and what is frequently misunderstood about each side’s strengths and weaknesses in the global artificial intelligence race.
This interview first appeared in SCMP Plus. For other interviews in the Open Questions series, click here.
Do you see the recent saga around Nvidia as a turning point for the China-US tech competition? Why or why not?
Yes and no. In the near term, the saga will have a significant impact on the competitive dynamics. Jensen Huang is the single most influential advocate for looser technology controls on China. Even with his reinstatement, he is unlikely to continue his advocacy due to intensified scrutiny and potential political backlash. The trajectory for US export controls on China is only going to be more hawkish, and we are already seeing the impact.
We have seen the release of the latest [US Bureau of Industry and Security] remote access rule, and the blacklist of [Singaporean cloud computing firm] Megaspeed and its related entities.
The new BIS rule targets not only China’s remote access to advanced AI computing power – which is expected to account for about one-third of China’s cumulative AI compute access by 2027 – but also diversion and Chinese AI chip designers’ access to overseas foundries. Its impact is therefore much broader than the headlines suggest.
If BIS strictly enforces the rule, including by declining many licences for access, China’s AI sector could suffer significant near-term pain because many doors to advanced AI computing power would effectively be shut.
Chinese companies would have little choice but to rely on their existing stock of restricted chips and domestic production. Supply through both channels is quite limited.
However, I do not think the Nvidia saga changes the long-term direction of US-China AI or technology competition. China’s push for semiconductor self-sufficiency has been under way for many years.
For Beijing, reducing reliance on foreign technology and building an indigenous Chinese technology stack has almost always been a priority – arguably as important as seeing Chinese AI labs dominate global benchmarks.
Before the Nvidia saga, Chinese AI companies preferred foreign chips because they were better. There was a degree of misalignment between the government’s priorities and what the companies wanted.
Now, with the saga and new restrictions, Chinese companies may have fewer fantasies about continued access to foreign chips and will more fully embrace domestic alternatives.
This will only accelerate the development of the domestic tech stack, because it will lead to more user feedback and kick off a positive feedback loop that helps them improve.
Regardless of what happens in the US, the Chinese government remains firmly committed to developing AI
What does Huang’s departure and comeback mean for global AI demand?
Huang is certainly irreplaceable and highly influential in the global AI sector. His comeback is good for Nvidia’s business and the global AI sector, but it does not resolve ongoing concerns over AI’s return on investment, circular financing, rising cost of capital or the changing political environment after the midterms.
One big variable is the new BIS remote-access rule.
If BIS enforces it very strictly, a lot of Chinese remote access to computing power could be cut off. We need to see whether those freed-up compute resources are easily reallocated.
[US President Donald Trump] has also made some bold claims on blocking US companies from building AI data centres overseas and imposing hefty taxes on firms that do so. This is contradictory to his diffusionist approach – but it’s Trump. If he does so, it will be really bad for US hyperscalers, as global diffusion is important if the US objective is to secure global leadership in AI before China catches up.
Compounded by the Democratic “blue wave,” we might see some slowdown in data centre buildouts and more market consolidation. However, that isn’t necessarily a bad thing – more disciplined, paced investment can be healthy for the industry in the long run.
If consolidation removes weaker players and weaker projects, it could also give US power infrastructure more time to catch up. Some estimates suggest that power constraints could become a serious bottleneck for US data-centre construction in late 2027 and 2028.
Another factor is US-China AI competition. Regardless of what happens in the US, the Chinese government remains firmly committed to developing AI.
Beijing appears to believe that AI is a transformative technology that can boost productivity, and it wants to diffuse AI across the economy and globally.
Competition between the US and China will give both countries strong incentives to sustain investment in AI.
[embedded media]
Does the new BIS rule change the nature of export controls?
I see the recent BIS rule less as a fundamental shift in the US approach and more as a very serious effort to close a loophole in existing export controls.
The US began limiting exports of advanced AI chips to China in October 2022, which focused on physical chips. However, until the latest BIS rule, remote access was considered legal.
That created an obvious policy gap. If Washington’s stated goal is to limit China’s access to advanced computing power, it does not make sense to limit physical chip exports while leaving the door wide open to remote access to those same chips.
My interpretation is that this contradiction was not necessarily the result of a calculated policy choice. It reflected incoherent policymaking in Washington and loopholes in the existing US export-control framework.
This was already a well-recognised loophole within Washington; Congress had been trying to close it since April 2024, when they first introduced the Remote Access Security Act.
So this whole Nvidia saga basically just added political urgency and accelerated that policy effort.
What does the new rule reveal about divisions in Washington?
There are two layers to the issue. One is potential corruption and knowing violations of export controls. There have been constant suspicions and speculation that improper business dealings or corruption may have been involved in the administration.
In my view, that is plausible, and we will find out more through the ongoing investigations.
The other layer is the debate over export controls themselves.
Export controls are difficult to calibrate. If they are too loose, they can give rivals the technology they need to improve their competitiveness and military capabilities, potentially threatening national security.
[embedded media]
But if controls are too restrictive, they can hurt the revenue of domestic companies and potentially weaken their ability to invest in research and development. They can also incentivise rivals to double down on innovation and develop alternative systems.
Trump officials and tech CEOs have been divided on this export control debate regarding advanced chips.
On one side, you have the hawks advocating for tighter controls on national security grounds; on the other, you have Trump, Huang and [White House adviser] David Sacks advocating for diffusing the American tech stack globally to secure American technological leadership, market share and global influence.
They believe that maintaining global influence will deter rivals such as Huawei Technologies from developing highly competitive alternative systems.
The middle ground they reached was permitting the export of the H200, which was Nvidia’s third- or fourth-best chip. But the Nvidia saga, which involved remote access and chip diversion, complicated that debate.
The export controls did not work as intended. What I want to highlight is that this debate between control and diffusion is highly legitimate and not unique to Washington.
As China ascends in various tech sectors, the Chinese government is also releasing technology export controls, and we can see from policy documents that Beijing is wrestling with the same balancing act.
Is the “small yard, high fence” expanding?
The yard is certainly getting bigger and the fence is getting higher. The problem is that the boundary is difficult to draw, because national security is a very broadly defined concept.
In export controls, I think the focus will gradually shift from restricting access to advanced chips – an area where the US has already done a great deal – to controls on semiconductor manufacturing equipment.
The argument is that if controls on equipment are looser than controls on the chips themselves, they will simply enable China to manufacture its own chips. That would undermine the purpose of the restrictions.
The US has already been implementing pretty strict equipment controls since 2022, though there are still loopholes in the framework.
[embedded media]
The bill to watch very closely will be the Match Act, which would force US allies to align with US export controls, with a special focus on advanced lithography machines from [Dutch equipment maker] ASML.
That bill would have major consequences because it would not only restrict more tool exports, but also potentially suspend components and services for existing advanced lithography systems, which would have a very damaging impact on China’s existing production capacity of advanced chips.
There is also a parallel concern in the US regarding Chinese products and components in US communications networks, infrastructure and supply chains.
The [US Federal Communications Commission] has been spearheading quite a bit of restriction there, targeting a wide range of Chinese imports.
We’re talking about things like drones, robots and power inverters, and now there is discussion about potentially blocking optical transceivers.
The FCC’s concerns revolve around data security, cybersecurity and over-reliance on Chinese supply chains, which they believe pose a significant national security threat.
Just as China is pursuing self-sufficiency, the US is pursuing very similar goals in strategic sectors.
Of course, there is a disconnect between policy ambitions and practical reality for both sides, but the trend of strategic decoupling at this point is irreversible.
How effective have US technology controls been?
The impact of these controls has been uneven, as the control regime on advanced-chip exports has proved quite porous because of remote access and chip diversion.
But one point I want to emphasise: even though China has continued to gain access through these channels, the restrictions have raised costs for Chinese AI companies and supply remains limited.
[embedded media]
As a result, we are seeing greater adoption of domestic chips. That is helping domestic products improve.
Compute constraints have also encouraged innovation in China in areas such as algorithms, model architecture, inference efficiency and compute-cluster management, because Chinese companies need to operate different types of chips within the same cluster and need to maximise utilisation of limited compute resources.
That progress will enhance the competitiveness of China’s technology stack.
However, controls on high-bandwidth memory (HBM) and semiconductor manufacturing equipment have created much greater challenges for China, because they directly affect China’s ability to expand onshore advanced chip manufacturing capacity.
Domestic HBM production is also constrained to a large extent by these tool restrictions. While these restrictions have certainly created fresh opportunities for domestic toolmakers – and Chinese toolmakers are indeed making progress in certain categories – many critical gaps remain.
I would caution against a common analogy between China’s semiconductor catch-up and its success in electric vehicles.
Advanced semiconductor manufacturing is perhaps the single most complex and globalised industrial process in the world, involving more than a thousand complex process steps and requiring hundreds of advanced tools to work reliably together.
The constraint isn’t just lithography, which always grabs the headlines; it spans a wide range of different tools, software and know-how. Foreign incumbents have spent decades accumulating this technology, know-how, IP and reliability track record.
So while I am confident in China’s ability to eventually make a breakthrough, I believe it will be a very lengthy and capital-intensive process.
Can opposition from US allies weaken the Match Act?
The Dutch government and ASML have consistently opposed tighter controls on the export of lithography machines to China. Under US pressure, however, the Dutch government agreed to restrictions on ASML’s advanced immersion-lithography systems.
My view is that opposition from the Dutch government as well as from ASML is unlikely to be the deciding factor. These parties have limited leverage.
Ultimately, the outcome will depend on Washington’s own assessment of the controls and on China’s response.
The single biggest variable to watch will be the outcome of the investigations into Nvidia and Huang
What is the outlook on tech after the US midterm elections?
I am not an expert on US politics, but I can share my views.
The various export controls on China have had bipartisan support. It is not just the Democrats; there is support across both parties.
The main people slowing these controls were Trump and a small number of his officials, as well as Jensen Huang and his lobbying efforts, because they were not fully on board for a variety of reasons.
My reading of the midterms is that China is not the central issue for Democrats. Their priorities are more likely to be affordability and inflation, investigating potential corruption in the Trump administration, ending the Iran war and ending the Russia-Ukraine war.
After January, however, I think the single biggest variable to watch will be the outcome of the investigations into Nvidia and Huang. Trump’s personal intervention to reinstate Huang as CEO has already invigorated the hawks and Democrats.
If the investigations uncover corruption or questionable business dealings within the administration, or serious export-control violations by Nvidia or Huang, that would almost certainly inject fresh momentum into a more hawkish US technology policy towards China. We could expect even tighter controls.
Will scrutiny spread to AMD and other US chipmakers?
Broadly speaking, the Nvidia saga is likely to attract fresh scrutiny of American companies with ties to China. Those ties could be personal or commercial, and investigators may examine whether business dealings are questionable.
In the semiconductor sector, the key question is whether there has been any transfer of technology or products, including chips, in violation of US export controls. There may also be other business dealings that are considered sensitive or impermissible under US rules.
AMD is an obvious target for scrutiny. I am not sure that this is because of personal ties. A more likely reason is that AMD is the second choice for Chinese buyers seeking advanced AI chips.
I had a quick skim of the original short-seller report. I think it contains some errors. AMD’s revenue in China does not come exclusively from AI chips. The company also sells a substantial amount of CPU products there. Those errors raise questions about the report’s credibility.
[embedded media]
I would also highlight that, shortly after China shut the door on Nvidia’s H200, AMD held a high-profile event involving its China business. It even advertised itself as “Advanced Mutual Development” at the event. AMD is clearly trying to capture some of the market share Nvidia has lost.
But that is not proof that AMD has done anything wrong. The Trump administration approved the export of some AMD chips to China.
Based on what I have heard from people on the ground, I have not heard of AMD chips being diverted. They are also not as desirable to Chinese buyers as Nvidia’s chips.
Where are China’s biggest vulnerabilities in AI and semiconductors?
Start with semiconductors. China can design chips, so chip design is not really the problem. It can also develop world-leading AI models, as we have already seen.
The constraint is advanced computing power, which is very important because data, algorithms and computing power are the three key elements of AI.
Now that the door to foreign chips is basically shut, hopes rest on domestic production. But I would describe the bottleneck as a whole-supply-chain problem for the advanced semiconductor stack.
China’s self-sufficiency across the entire stack – ranging from advanced tools and their critical components to advanced semiconductor materials, electronic design automation tools and packaging – still depends heavily on foreign technologies and suppliers.
As for the AI stack, China has done a very good job in algorithmic innovation, inference efficiency and cost management.
China also claims to have a major advantage in data because it has a huge manufacturing base and many industries operating domestically.
That creates data availability. But Chinese industrial data is often fragmented and not standardised, so it is not necessarily ready for model training.
That is why the Chinese government is orchestrating a top-down effort to collect and organise high-quality data sets. If that effort succeeds, China could have a considerable advantage in this area.
[embedded media]
Monetisation is definitely important. Data is expensive, and AI compute, safety testing and experimental research are expensive.
Given the current technology sell-off and the persistent monetisation challenges facing Chinese AI models, the question of how these companies will generate returns is an important one.
How are Chinese AI companies monetising their technology?
Monetisation is different for hyperscalers such as ByteDance and [South China Morning Post owner] Alibaba, compared with independent AI labs. For independent labs, their main revenue sources are local deployment services or application programming interfaces (APIs).
Looking at the financials of listed labs, they are deriving an increasing proportion of their revenue from overseas. The question is whether that overseas revenue is sustainable given the new controls.
Even with overseas sales, their API revenue remains very small compared with the US frontier labs, raising the question of whether they can generate enough revenue to recover their costs.
For the hyperscalers like ByteDance, it’s a two-part story.
First, they incorporate AI into internal business to improve efficiency and generate more revenue, including through e-commerce and advertising.
Second, companies like ByteDance and Alibaba pursue a full-stack strategy offering cloud services, leveraging their compute resources to provide models-as-a-service.
Alibaba’s earnings have already shown that the margins from providing its own models and third-party models are very similar. As long as a company has computing resources, it can monetise them.
The other area is stand-alone AI applications. There is still limited evidence that these applications can generate sufficient revenue.
That is due to several factors, including consumers’ low willingness to pay in China and intense competition among companies, with subsidies and price competition.
In the near term, as long as the US continues to push global diffusion, the US is likely to hold the upper hand
One bright spot is video generation models, particularly from ByteDance, which benefit from vertical integration across content distribution and video models.
They have done well, though a major downstream application of video models – microdramas – is becoming extremely cutthroat and crowded. So there are still questions about how sustainable that growth is going forward.
Lastly, revenue could come from AI hardware. China has a very strong manufacturing supply chain and cost advantage.
It can produce hardware at scale and add AI capabilities to it. There could be decent opportunities if China can produce attractive AI hardware.
Just like in other manufacturing sectors, even if the domestic market doesn’t generate high margins, companies can export overseas where there is plenty of demand. That’s definitely a space to watch.
Which country is better positioned to export its AI stack globally?
The practical problem is that China does not yet have a complete AI stack that it can export at scale because it lacks advanced chips.
Even if Chinese models are adopted, they often run on US chips, including in [Belt and Road Initiative] countries. That is still a significant disadvantage.
China’s limited onshore production of advanced chips will remain a substantial bottleneck to diffusing its AI stack in the near term, and that likely won’t be resolved in the next two to three years.
Furthermore, with the crackdown on model distillation and remote access, there are questions about how fast Chinese models can continue advancing.
Chinese companies can still generate revenue by providing local deployment services for smaller models running on existing hardware, but in the near term, as long as the US continues to push global diffusion, the US is likely to hold the upper hand.
[embedded media]
Can China eventually replace advanced US chips?
All these challenges and workarounds come down to the same fundamental issue: chip manufacturing.
Even if you use a supernode architecture to compensate for lower single-chip performance by networking many chips together, you still need a massive volume of chips, so it again comes down to chip manufacturing.
You can design these architectures on paper and in theory, but the real test is whether you can mass-produce them in volume using reliable equipment in a profitable manner.
Profitability is secondary here – the core question is mass production, which brings us right back to China’s lag in advanced semiconductor equipment.
Catching up in equipment isn’t easy. Beyond technology and know-how, you face strict IP walls, and even after building a tool, it takes at least two to three years of reliability testing to achieve the desired yields.
So there are no quick short cuts in moving forward. However, because of these constraints, China will definitely double down on exploring all alternative pathways, and by concentrating a whole-of-nation effort, it may eventually find breakthroughs.
Where could China make the biggest breakthroughs in semiconductor equipment?
In equipment, China may have a better chance of making progress in areas where demand is greatest.
For instance, etching, deposition and hybrid bonding tools. There are still substantial gaps, but these tools are needed for multiple critical applications, so China may be able to mobilise more resources and effort. There are also some good Chinese companies in these areas.
Breakthroughs in advanced lithography, particularly extreme ultraviolet lithography, will be extremely difficult. Inspection and metrology equipment will also be very tough nuts to crack.
[embedded media]
Does China have an energy advantage in AI?
I think China’s energy advantage in AI is somewhat overstated.
Energy is very important. China’s power grid is the world’s largest and one of its most advanced, and it continues to add generation capacity.
But China’s electricity advantage is not so much about the cost of electricity; it is about the availability of energy.
Another point that is often misunderstood is the share of electricity in data-centre costs.
Electricity accounts for about one-quarter of the annual operating expenditure of a US data centre.
But if you factor in both operating expenditure and capital expenditure, electricity accounts for only about 7 per cent of the all-in annual cost of a US data centre.
So even if China has an overwhelming advantage in electricity costs, that may not matter as much as people think.
The bulk of the all-in cost – around 60 per cent – is the servers, where China does not have an advantage.
That said, power availability will matter a great deal if the US hits grid bottlenecks.
We could end up with a very interesting dynamic in the coming years: China builds plenty of data centres with abundant power, waiting on advanced chips, while the US has plenty of advanced chips, waiting on power.
Rare earths have genuinely been China’s trump card, and their potency will last well into the foreseeable future
How effective are China’s rare earth countermeasures?
Trump’s claim [of catching up with China in rare earth in 10 months] is highly exaggerated.
Rare earths have genuinely been China’s trump card, and their potency will last well into the foreseeable future.
Even though we are seeing concerted efforts by the US and its allies to build alternative supply chains, that will be a very lengthy process.
Japan is probably the best example. Even after about 15 years of effort, Japan – a technologically advanced country – has only reduced its dependence on China for rare earth imports from around 90 per cent in 2010 to about 65 to 70 per cent today.
This shows that while China’s leverage may diminish gradually over time, substantially eliminating it is a multi-decade endeavour.
A realistic assessment for the US is that it could achieve high self-sufficiency in rare earths for the defence sector within two to three years, since defence volumes are relatively small.
However, it is likely to take 10 years or more for the US to reduce its dependence on Chinese rare earths across broader civilian sectors.
That matters enormously because we are talking about critical materials used across countless civilian applications, including the semiconductor industry itself.
Unlike US export controls on chips and equipment, China’s dominance in rare earths can have an immediate effect on global supply chains. China has been approving export licences selectively and incrementally, using that process to extend its leverage.
So far, that approach appears to have worked, as we have seen in the back-and-forth in bilateral relations.
[embedded media]
Is there room for understanding in the US-China technology trade?
Strategic decoupling is mutual and is an irreversible trend, as we have discussed. Both sides are working to reduce their strategic dependence on each other.
But there is certainly room to reach some kind of consensus to maintain stability during this period – what’s been called “constructive strategic stability.”
The problem is that, although we have learned that escalation is not sustainable, there appears to be a persistent underestimation in Washington of China’s ability and willingness to retaliate.
Perhaps US policymakers will need to experience more rounds of escalation before they learn that lesson.
The Match Act will be a good test. China has already vowed to retaliate, and I think it will do so because of the impact the legislation could have.
We will see how that plays out, and perhaps it will bring the discussion back to constructive strategic stability.
[embedded media]
What’s the export outlook for Chinese AI commercial applications and less advanced chips?
Commercial applications are complicated because of data-security concerns.
We have already seen how those issues played out in the TikTok dispute. It depends on the application and its nature. Video-editing applications, for example, may be treated differently.
There are already Chinese video-editing apps available in the US, whereas an app such as TikTok may not be acceptable. It will be assessed case by case, depending on data security and concerns about propaganda.
As for mature semiconductors, I think this is an area that will attract growing scrutiny from the US.
China is expanding its production capacity very quickly, largely without the equipment export controls that apply to advanced manufacturing.
China’s share of global mature-chip production capacity is expected to rise from about one-third in 2024 to more than half by 2030.
This matters because, although mature chips do not require advanced process technology, they are widely used in both defence and non-defence applications. Mature semiconductors account for more than 90 per cent of global chip sales by volume.
It is therefore almost inevitable that the US will increase scrutiny of this area, given China’s potential leverage to disrupt global supply chains.
By Ben Jiang, Ji Siqi

There is also a parallel concern in the US regarding Chinese products and components in US communications networks, infrastructure and supply chains.
The [US Federal Communications Commission] has been spearheading quite a bit of restriction there, targeting a wide range of Chinese imports.
We’re talking about things like drones, robots and power inverters, and now there is discussion about potentially blocking optical transceivers.
The FCC’s concerns revolve around data security, cybersecurity and over-reliance on Chinese supply chains, which they believe pose a significant national security threat.
Just as China is pursuing self-sufficiency, the US is pursuing very similar goals in strategic sectors.
Of course, there is a disconnect between policy ambitions and practical reality for both sides, but the trend of strategic decoupling at this point is irreversible.
How effective have US technology controls been?
The impact of these controls has been uneven, as the control regime on advanced-chip exports has proved quite porous because of remote access and chip diversion.
But one point I want to emphasise: even though China has continued to gain access through these channels, the restrictions have raised costs for Chinese AI companies and supply remains limited.
[embedded media]
As a result, we are seeing greater adoption of domestic chips. That is helping domestic products improve.
Compute constraints have also encouraged innovation in China in areas such as algorithms, model architecture, inference efficiency and compute-cluster management, because Chinese companies need to operate different types of chips within the same cluster and need to maximise utilisation of limited compute resources.
That progress will enhance the competitiveness of China’s technology stack.
However, controls on high-bandwidth memory (HBM) and semiconductor manufacturing equipment have created much greater challenges for China, because they directly affect China’s ability to expand onshore advanced chip manufacturing capacity.
Domestic HBM production is also constrained to a large extent by these tool restrictions. While these restrictions have certainly created fresh opportunities for domestic toolmakers – and Chinese toolmakers are indeed making progress in certain categories – many critical gaps remain.
I would caution against a common analogy between China’s semiconductor catch-up and its success in electric vehicles.
Advanced semiconductor manufacturing is perhaps the single most complex and globalised industrial process in the world, involving more than a thousand complex process steps and requiring hundreds of advanced tools to work reliably together.
The constraint isn’t just lithography, which always grabs the headlines; it spans a wide range of different tools, software and know-how. Foreign incumbents have spent decades accumulating this technology, know-how, IP and reliability track record.
So while I am confident in China’s ability to eventually make a breakthrough, I believe it will be a very lengthy and capital-intensive process.
Can opposition from US allies weaken the Match Act?
The Dutch government and ASML have consistently opposed tighter controls on the export of lithography machines to China. Under US pressure, however, the Dutch government agreed to restrictions on ASML’s advanced immersion-lithography systems.
My view is that opposition from the Dutch government as well as from ASML is unlikely to be the deciding factor. These parties have limited leverage.
Ultimately, the outcome will depend on Washington’s own assessment of the controls and on China’s response.
The single biggest variable to watch will be the outcome of the investigations into Nvidia and Huang
What is the outlook on tech after the US midterm elections?
I am not an expert on US politics, but I can share my views.
The various export controls on China have had bipartisan support. It is not just the Democrats; there is support across both parties.
The main people slowing these controls were Trump and a small number of his officials, as well as Jensen Huang and his lobbying efforts, because they were not fully on board for a variety of reasons.
My reading of the midterms is that China is not the central issue for Democrats. Their priorities are more likely to be affordability and inflation, investigating potential corruption in the Trump administration, ending the Iran war and ending the Russia-Ukraine war.
After January, however, I think the single biggest variable to watch will be the outcome of the investigations into Nvidia and Huang. Trump’s personal intervention to reinstate Huang as CEO has already invigorated the hawks and Democrats.
If the investigations uncover corruption or questionable business dealings within the administration, or serious export-control violations by Nvidia or Huang, that would almost certainly inject fresh momentum into a more hawkish US technology policy towards China. We could expect even tighter controls.
Will scrutiny spread to AMD and other US chipmakers?
Broadly speaking, the Nvidia saga is likely to attract fresh scrutiny of American companies with ties to China. Those ties could be personal or commercial, and investigators may examine whether business dealings are questionable.
In the semiconductor sector, the key question is whether there has been any transfer of technology or products, including chips, in violation of US export controls. There may also be other business dealings that are considered sensitive or impermissible under US rules.
AMD is an obvious target for scrutiny. I am not sure that this is because of personal ties. A more likely reason is that AMD is the second choice for Chinese buyers seeking advanced AI chips.
I had a quick skim of the original short-seller report. I think it contains some errors. AMD’s revenue in China does not come exclusively from AI chips. The company also sells a substantial amount of CPU products there. Those errors raise questions about the report’s credibility.
[embedded media]
I would also highlight that, shortly after China shut the door on Nvidia’s H200, AMD held a high-profile event involving its China business. It even advertised itself as “Advanced Mutual Development” at the event. AMD is clearly trying to capture some of the market share Nvidia has lost.
But that is not proof that AMD has done anything wrong. The Trump administration approved the export of some AMD chips to China.
Based on what I have heard from people on the ground, I have not heard of AMD chips being diverted. They are also not as desirable to Chinese buyers as Nvidia’s chips.
Where are China’s biggest vulnerabilities in AI and semiconductors?
Start with semiconductors. China can design chips, so chip design is not really the problem. It can also develop world-leading AI models, as we have already seen.
The constraint is advanced computing power, which is very important because data, algorithms and computing power are the three key elements of AI.
Now that the door to foreign chips is basically shut, hopes rest on domestic production. But I would describe the bottleneck as a whole-supply-chain problem for the advanced semiconductor stack.
China’s self-sufficiency across the entire stack – ranging from advanced tools and their critical components to advanced semiconductor materials, electronic design automation tools and packaging – still depends heavily on foreign technologies and suppliers.
As for the AI stack, China has done a very good job in algorithmic innovation, inference efficiency and cost management.
China also claims to have a major advantage in data because it has a huge manufacturing base and many industries operating domestically.
That creates data availability. But Chinese industrial data is often fragmented and not standardised, so it is not necessarily ready for model training.
That is why the Chinese government is orchestrating a top-down effort to collect and organise high-quality data sets. If that effort succeeds, China could have a considerable advantage in this area.
[embedded media]
Monetisation is definitely important. Data is expensive, and AI compute, safety testing and experimental research are expensive.
Given the current technology sell-off and the persistent monetisation challenges facing Chinese AI models, the question of how these companies will generate returns is an important one.
How are Chinese AI companies monetising their technology?
Monetisation is different for hyperscalers such as ByteDance and [South China Morning Post owner] Alibaba, compared with independent AI labs. For independent labs, their main revenue sources are local deployment services or application programming interfaces (APIs).
Looking at the financials of listed labs, they are deriving an increasing proportion of their revenue from overseas. The question is whether that overseas revenue is sustainable given the new controls.
Even with overseas sales, their API revenue remains very small compared with the US frontier labs, raising the question of whether they can generate enough revenue to recover their costs.
For the hyperscalers like ByteDance, it’s a two-part story.
First, they incorporate AI into internal business to improve efficiency and generate more revenue, including through e-commerce and advertising.
Second, companies like ByteDance and Alibaba pursue a full-stack strategy offering cloud services, leveraging their compute resources to provide models-as-a-service.
Alibaba’s earnings have already shown that the margins from providing its own models and third-party models are very similar. As long as a company has computing resources, it can monetise them.
The other area is stand-alone AI applications. There is still limited evidence that these applications can generate sufficient revenue.
That is due to several factors, including consumers’ low willingness to pay in China and intense competition among companies, with subsidies and price competition.
In the near term, as long as the US continues to push global diffusion, the US is likely to hold the upper hand
One bright spot is video generation models, particularly from ByteDance, which benefit from vertical integration across content distribution and video models.
They have done well, though a major downstream application of video models – microdramas – is becoming extremely cutthroat and crowded. So there are still questions about how sustainable that growth is going forward.
Lastly, revenue could come from AI hardware. China has a very strong manufacturing supply chain and cost advantage.
It can produce hardware at scale and add AI capabilities to it. There could be decent opportunities if China can produce attractive AI hardware.
Just like in other manufacturing sectors, even if the domestic market doesn’t generate high margins, companies can export overseas where there is plenty of demand. That’s definitely a space to watch.
Which country is better positioned to export its AI stack globally?
The practical problem is that China does not yet have a complete AI stack that it can export at scale because it lacks advanced chips.
Even if Chinese models are adopted, they often run on US chips, including in [Belt and Road Initiative] countries. That is still a significant disadvantage.
China’s limited onshore production of advanced chips will remain a substantial bottleneck to diffusing its AI stack in the near term, and that likely won’t be resolved in the next two to three years.
Furthermore, with the crackdown on model distillation and remote access, there are questions about how fast Chinese models can continue advancing.
Chinese companies can still generate revenue by providing local deployment services for smaller models running on existing hardware, but in the near term, as long as the US continues to push global diffusion, the US is likely to hold the upper hand.
[embedded media]
Can China eventually replace advanced US chips?
All these challenges and workarounds come down to the same fundamental issue: chip manufacturing.
Even if you use a supernode architecture to compensate for lower single-chip performance by networking many chips together, you still need a massive volume of chips, so it again comes down to chip manufacturing.
You can design these architectures on paper and in theory, but the real test is whether you can mass-produce them in volume using reliable equipment in a profitable manner.
Profitability is secondary here – the core question is mass production, which brings us right back to China’s lag in advanced semiconductor equipment.
Catching up in equipment isn’t easy. Beyond technology and know-how, you face strict IP walls, and even after building a tool, it takes at least two to three years of reliability testing to achieve the desired yields.
So there are no quick short cuts in moving forward. However, because of these constraints, China will definitely double down on exploring all alternative pathways, and by concentrating a whole-of-nation effort, it may eventually find breakthroughs.
Where could China make the biggest breakthroughs in semiconductor equipment?
In equipment, China may have a better chance of making progress in areas where demand is greatest.
For instance, etching, deposition and hybrid bonding tools. There are still substantial gaps, but these tools are needed for multiple critical applications, so China may be able to mobilise more resources and effort. There are also some good Chinese companies in these areas.
Breakthroughs in advanced lithography, particularly extreme ultraviolet lithography, will be extremely difficult. Inspection and metrology equipment will also be very tough nuts to crack.
[embedded media]
Does China have an energy advantage in AI?
I think China’s energy advantage in AI is somewhat overstated.
Energy is very important. China’s power grid is the world’s largest and one of its most advanced, and it continues to add generation capacity.
But China’s electricity advantage is not so much about the cost of electricity; it is about the availability of energy.
Another point that is often misunderstood is the share of electricity in data-centre costs.
Electricity accounts for about one-quarter of the annual operating expenditure of a US data centre.
But if you factor in both operating expenditure and capital expenditure, electricity accounts for only about 7 per cent of the all-in annual cost of a US data centre.
So even if China has an overwhelming advantage in electricity costs, that may not matter as much as people think.
The bulk of the all-in cost – around 60 per cent – is the servers, where China does not have an advantage.
That said, power availability will matter a great deal if the US hits grid bottlenecks.
We could end up with a very interesting dynamic in the coming years: China builds plenty of data centres with abundant power, waiting on advanced chips, while the US has plenty of advanced chips, waiting on power.
Rare earths have genuinely been China’s trump card, and their potency will last well into the foreseeable future
How effective are China’s rare earth countermeasures?
Trump’s claim [of catching up with China in rare earth in 10 months] is highly exaggerated.
Rare earths have genuinely been China’s trump card, and their potency will last well into the foreseeable future.
Even though we are seeing concerted efforts by the US and its allies to build alternative supply chains, that will be a very lengthy process.
Japan is probably the best example. Even after about 15 years of effort, Japan – a technologically advanced country – has only reduced its dependence on China for rare earth imports from around 90 per cent in 2010 to about 65 to 70 per cent today.
This shows that while China’s leverage may diminish gradually over time, substantially eliminating it is a multi-decade endeavour.
A realistic assessment for the US is that it could achieve high self-sufficiency in rare earths for the defence sector within two to three years, since defence volumes are relatively small.
However, it is likely to take 10 years or more for the US to reduce its dependence on Chinese rare earths across broader civilian sectors.
That matters enormously because we are talking about critical materials used across countless civilian applications, including the semiconductor industry itself.
Unlike US export controls on chips and equipment, China’s dominance in rare earths can have an immediate effect on global supply chains. China has been approving export licences selectively and incrementally, using that process to extend its leverage.
So far, that approach appears to have worked, as we have seen in the back-and-forth in bilateral relations.
[embedded media]
Is there room for understanding in the US-China technology trade?
Strategic decoupling is mutual and is an irreversible trend, as we have discussed. Both sides are working to reduce their strategic dependence on each other.
But there is certainly room to reach some kind of consensus to maintain stability during this period – what’s been called “constructive strategic stability.”
The problem is that, although we have learned that escalation is not sustainable, there appears to be a persistent underestimation in Washington of China’s ability and willingness to retaliate.
Perhaps US policymakers will need to experience more rounds of escalation before they learn that lesson.
The Match Act will be a good test. China has already vowed to retaliate, and I think it will do so because of the impact the legislation could have.
We will see how that plays out, and perhaps it will bring the discussion back to constructive strategic stability.
[embedded media]
What’s the export outlook for Chinese AI commercial applications and less advanced chips?
Commercial applications are complicated because of data-security concerns.
We have already seen how those issues played out in the TikTok dispute. It depends on the application and its nature. Video-editing applications, for example, may be treated differently.
There are already Chinese video-editing apps available in the US, whereas an app such as TikTok may not be acceptable. It will be assessed case by case, depending on data security and concerns about propaganda.
As for mature semiconductors, I think this is an area that will attract growing scrutiny from the US.
China is expanding its production capacity very quickly, largely without the equipment export controls that apply to advanced manufacturing.
China’s share of global mature-chip production capacity is expected to rise from about one-third in 2024 to more than half by 2030.
This matters because, although mature chips do not require advanced process technology, they are widely used in both defence and non-defence applications. Mature semiconductors account for more than 90 per cent of global chip sales by volume.
It is therefore almost inevitable that the US will increase scrutiny of this area, given China’s potential leverage to disrupt global supply chains.
By Ben Jiang, Ji Siqi

title_en: Let’s keep doing lunch: Hong Kong exchange leans towards keeping noon break, sources say
content_en:
HKEX sees no turnover upside in ending the mid-day break, but adjusting opening and closing times is up for discussion, multiple sources say.
People pass Exchange Square, home to bourse operator Hong Kong Exchanges and Clearing, on July 17. Photo: Karma Lo
Lunch is likely to remain on the menu for Hong Kong stock brokers, as the city’s bourse operator leans towards extending trading hours at either end of the day while keeping the market’s traditional mid-day break intact, according to multiple sources.
Hong Kong Exchanges and Clearing (HKEX) will not highlight the idea of cancelling the current hour-long noon break when it issues a discussion paper on its operating hours as early as next week, sources with knowledge of the matter told the South China Morning Post. Having the market open earlier or stay open later, or both, would be discussed, they said.
The paper, expected ahead of the Nasdaq’s extension to 23-hour trading on December 6, would elicit views on the overall direction of any change before a detailed consultation at a later stage, a source said.
“While other markets such as the US, UK and South Korea have, or will have, plans to extend their trading times, Hong Kong cannot keep the status quo,” the source said. “But we have to discuss how to catch up.”
The lunch break would be spared because the exchange did not believe trading during that hour would significantly increase turnover, the source said.
“The lunch break in Hong Kong from noon to 1pm Hong Kong time does not overlap with other markets,” the source said. “As such, it would not bring much more turnover from overseas investors even if the lunch break were cancelled.”
Hong Kong’s stock market currently trades from 9.30am to 4pm, with the hour lunch break from noon. Photo: Jelly Tse
A second source said the discussion paper would ask whether the market should extend its hours in the morning and evening to overlap with other markets and capture investors from those markets.
“Opening the Hong Kong stock market earlier would overlap our trading hours with Japan and South Korea, while closing the market later would help capture trading from Europe and the UK,” the second source said.
A third source said that the Stock Connect mechanism, which allows cross-border trading, would be an important consideration for any changes to trading hours.
Hong Kong’s stock market currently trades from 9.30am to 4pm, with the hour lunch break from noon, while the stock markets in Shanghai and Shenzhen trade from 9.30am to 3pm, with a 1.5 hour break starting at 11.30am.
“Southbound trading via Stock Connect now represents a significant portion of the turnover in Hong Kong,” the third source said. “As such, any change in Hong Kong must have Stock Connect schemes in mind.”
At some point [the lunch break] has to go for Hong Kong to compete with the other marketsDavid Friedland, Interactive Brokers Group
A spokesman for HKEX said the exchange was committed to enhancing market accessibility, noting its earlier decision to extend after-hours trading of derivatives to 4.15am from 3am starting in March 2027.
“HKEX recognises the importance of balancing the needs of different market stakeholders for any changes to the cash market’s trading hours,” the spokesman said. “We will publish a discussion paper in due course.”
Stephen Hui Chiu-chung, chairman and CEO of Hong Kong-based broker Luk Fook Financial Services, said he agreed with a minor extension to trading hours.
“A much longer trading session is not necessary, as it might not improve market turnover but would certainly add operating costs for the brokerage industry,” Hui said, also noting the importance of Stock Connect.
“If Hong Kong alone extends trading hours while the mainland bourse does not follow, it would not help boost turnover,” he said.
David Friedland, Hong Kong-based Asia-Pacific managing director at Interactive Brokers Group, said keeping the lunch break would limit the exchange’s competitiveness.
“The small brokers are going to push very hard to maintain the lunch break, even though at some point it has to go for Hong Kong to compete with the other markets,” Friedland said.
Longer trading hours in the US represented “a real competitive threat for Hong Kong”, he said, adding that ideally mainland China’s exchanges would consider extending their hours as well to expand Stock Connect’s availability.
By Enoch Yiu

title_en: UK man convicted of knife rampage on London-bound train
content_en:
Anthony Williams, 33, was found guilty of 14 counts of attempted murder for last year’s mass stabbing.
Anthony Williams appears via video link at Cambridge Crown Court on Thursday. Courtroom sketch: Elizabeth Cook/PA via AP
A man who went on the rampage armed with a knife on a London-bound train was on Thursday found guilty of the attempted murder of 14 people.
A jury found Anthony Williams, 33, guilty of all 10 counts of attempted murder on the train involving passengers and an on-board staff member, as well as earlier incidents in London and another UK town in which four others were injured.
Rail worker Samir Zitouni, 48 – who tried to stop Williams with a frying pan and was critically injured in the November 2025 attack – has been hailed for trying to protect passengers.
Williams had denied all 14 charges but admitted having intended to harm people.
Prosecutor Christopher Paxton earlier told the jury at Cambridge Crown Court in eastern England that over Halloween weekend last year Williams had “posed a dangerous threat, marauding through towns and cities, on streets and trains alike, armed with a knife”.
“He stabbed many, seeking to end their lives with deadly intention, striking out at them when they were defenceless and in fear,” he said.
Anthony Williams is seen in an undated custody photograph. Photo: British Transport Police via AFP
The mass stabbing happened on a train from Doncaster to London on the evening of November 1.
As the events unfolded, the driver made an emergency stop at Huntingdon in Cambridgeshire, where armed officers swarmed the station.
The trapped “passengers ran for their lives, hiding away in locked toilets, store cabinets or under seats” until many simply “ran out of train” and could go no further, Paxton said.
Some showed “extraordinary bravery” in trying to fend Williams off, grabbing pans or toasters to protect themselves, he said.
Williams did not give evidence at his trial and he appeared via video-link from Rampton Hospital, a high-security psychiatric hospital in Nottinghamshire.
Detective Superintendent Sam Blackburn, of the British Transport Police’s Major, Serious and Organised Crime Unit, said despite the incident, Britain’s trains were very safe.
“It’s incredibly rare for individuals to be involved in violence on the railway,” he said.
“Millions of passengers use the railway every single day. It is a safe and secure network.”
By Agence France-Presse

title_en: Spain’s Pablo Hernandez de Cos to succeed Lagarde as European Central Bank chief
content_en:
His nomination comes at a time of tension on European bond markets and before a series of high-stakes elections in Europe next year.
Pablo Hernandez de Cos speaks in Madrid, Spain, in May 2024. Photo: EPA
Spain’s Pablo Hernandez de Cos will be the next head of the European Central Bank, taking over from Christine Lagarde, diplomats said on Thursday.
His nomination comes at a time of tension on European bond markets and before a series of high-stakes elections in Europe next year, including in France.
Hernandez de Cos, 55, has been head of the Swiss-based Bank for International Settlements (BIS) since last year, and previously led the Bank of Spain from 2018 to 2024.
The ECB is the central bank for the 21 countries that use the euro, setting interest rates that influence borrowing costs across the economy, from mortgages to credit-card repayments.
“The Netherlands will support the consensus for the three nominations for the ECB board,” an EU diplomat said.
European Central Bank President Christine Lagarde attends a press conference in Frankfurt, Germany, in October. Photo: Reuters
That diplomat and a second confirmed it meant Hernandez de Cos won the support of euro area countries over Klaas Knot, former head of the Dutch central bank.
In addition to the ECB top job, France’s Laurence Boone and Germany’s Markus Brunnermeier were the sole candidates to fill two vacant seats on the bank’s executive board.
Thanks to a grand bargain on the package between France and Germany, Hernandez de Cos was chosen in a decision that came after EU leaders’ talks in Brussels.
Dutch Prime Minister Rob Jetten on Thursday informed European Council chief Antonio Costa “that the Netherlands values a consensual decision on the ECB presidency. An important signal to financial markets”, a diplomat said.
The Frankfurt-based institution has said Lagarde would step down in February 2027, several months before her term expires in October next year.
Lagarde was given a warm welcome during the summit, with leaders lavishing praise on her tenure, an official said.
Thursday’s green light triggers a formal process during which European leaders will later in the day approve the candidates for each ECB post.
The bank’s governing council and European Parliament will then formally back the nominations.
A campaign poster for Pedro Sanchez is displayed ahead of Spain’s general elections in the town of Olivas de La Frontera in Extremadura on Monday. Photo: Reuters
Spain’s Socialist Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez, who is battling unfavourable polling before a general election on Sunday, hailed the choice on social media, saying it reflects “a Spain that leads in Europe”.
He pointed to the Spanish chief of the European Investment Bank, Nadia Calvino, and the EU executive’s second most senior official, Teresa Ribera, as other figures of influence.
Known as a consensus builder, Hernandez de Cos is a career central banker whose pragmatic approach has earned him respect.
He is no stranger to crises after steering the Spanish central bank through the Covid-19 pandemic and the economic fallout from Russia’s 2022 invasion of Ukraine, which fuelled inflation and greater pressure on public finances.

title_display: Spain’s Pablo Hernandez de Cos to succeed Lagarde as European Central Bank chief
content_display:
His nomination comes at a time of tension on European bond markets and before a series of high-stakes elections in Europe next year.
Pablo Hernandez de Cos speaks in Madrid, Spain, in May 2024. Photo: EPA
Spain’s Pablo Hernandez de Cos will be the next head of the European Central Bank, taking over from Christine Lagarde, diplomats said on Thursday.
His nomination comes at a time of tension on European bond markets and before a series of high-stakes elections in Europe next year, including in France.
Hernandez de Cos, 55, has been head of the Swiss-based Bank for International Settlements (BIS) since last year, and previously led the Bank of Spain from 2018 to 2024.
The ECB is the central bank for the 21 countries that use the euro, setting interest rates that influence borrowing costs across the economy, from mortgages to credit-card repayments.
“The Netherlands will support the consensus for the three nominations for the ECB board,” an EU diplomat said.
European Central Bank President Christine Lagarde attends a press conference in Frankfurt, Germany, in October. Photo: Reuters
That diplomat and a second confirmed it meant Hernandez de Cos won the support of euro area countries over Klaas Knot, former head of the Dutch central bank.
In addition to the ECB top job, France’s Laurence Boone and Germany’s Markus Brunnermeier were the sole candidates to fill two vacant seats on the bank’s executive board.
Thanks to a grand bargain on the package between France and Germany, Hernandez de Cos was chosen in a decision that came after EU leaders’ talks in Brussels.
Dutch Prime Minister Rob Jetten on Thursday informed European Council chief Antonio Costa “that the Netherlands values a consensual decision on the ECB presidency. An important signal to financial markets”, a diplomat said.
The Frankfurt-based institution has said Lagarde would step down in February 2027, several months before her term expires in October next year.
Lagarde was given a warm welcome during the summit, with leaders lavishing praise on her tenure, an official said.
Thursday’s green light triggers a formal process during which European leaders will later in the day approve the candidates for each ECB post.
The bank’s governing council and European Parliament will then formally back the nominations.

title_en: Trump calls GDP figures ‘fake’, demands probe of his own Commerce Department
content_en:
The US president claimed bad data was purposefully released, linking it to his party’s poor performance in the recent midterm elections.
US President Donald Trump gestures during a press conference at the White House on November 20. Photo: Reuters
US President Donald Trump on Thursday accused his Commerce Department of purposely issuing incorrect economic growth figures before the midterm elections and said he wants to launch an investigation.
Trump has repeatedly sought to undermine trust in economic data that fails to match his claims of a historic boom, a pattern that threatens the credibility of figures needed by businesses, financial markets and consumers when making investments.
His latest complaint concerns data issued by the Commerce Department on Wednesday that revised gross domestic product in the third quarter to 4.3 per cent on an annual basis, up from a prior estimate of 3.4 per cent.
The department’s Bureau of Economic Analysis routinely updates its economic data to improve its accuracy. GDP figures, monthly jobs reports and other data are regularly revised. Those updates occur on a pre-scheduled basis without regard to the political calendar.
But the president claimed on social media that it was a “massive, and purposeful, error” and linked it to the poor performance for Republicans in the November 3 midterm elections that gave Democrats control of both houses of Congress.
[embedded media]
“It was just revealed that the REAL Numbers on the Economy, published before the Election, were FAKE, and a correction was issued yesterday by the people in the Government Agency that does these numbers,” Trump posted.
“Why wasn’t the correct number issued before the Election? I am asking for an immediate investigation of this situation.”
The Commerce Department did not immediately respond to a request for comment. The government is largely closed on Thursday for the Thanksgiving holiday.
This is the latest instance of Trump questioning the integrity of economic data he feels is unfavourable to him without providing evidence that revisions are politically motivated.
In August 2025, Trump fired the head of the Bureau of Labour Statistics after a decidedly weak jobs report. That report said only 73,000 jobs were added in July 2025 and showed that 258,000 fewer jobs were added in May and June than previously reported.
Trump called that jobs report “phony” and “rigged”.
Trump has claimed that he deserves credit for powering stronger economic growth, but voters do not share the president’s belief that the economy is strong.
In the midterms, 76 per cent described economic conditions as “not so good” or “poor”, according to the AP Voter Poll, an extensive survey of the electorate. About two-thirds of voters said Trump’s own policies had fuelled inflation.
The president in his social media post ignored that the same federal agency on Wednesday also reported that a key measure of inflation – the personal consumption expenditures price index – accelerated to an annual pace of 3.8 per cent in October.
By Associated Press
